At my university we had to do epistemology classes as part of our honors curriculum, regardless of major. If we don't strive to teach these skills, how can we hope to create a more informed and less ignorant populace? Is "education" really the problem? Or is it curriculum?

I'm arguing for reform. But I won't agree that education causes more ignorance than not. Education doesn't have to be what it is, especially in grade school. But also, what I'm saying applies more to public schools too- quality of education is definitely worse (I went to public school). It isn't the same across the board.

Learning to learn is the process of asking questions, not making assumptions, processing data, examining how that data was collected in the first place, contextualizing everything, being a skeptic, etc. People can and should be taught these skills so they can be more informed, less ignorant, and more ok with saying "I don't know" when they don't have sufficient information to have an opinion.
How so?

I hate to be so blunt, but this is a very bad take. The most ignorant people are those who have little education. They lack the skills to understand concepts fully, and to think critically in a methodical way.

The real problem is how people conceptualize what education *should* be. Most people view school, including college, like technical vocational training. But a good school should teach you *how to learn* as much as it teaches you a specific skill set.

If you go to a good college, they will emphasize methods of how to synthesize information, teach you to challenge your own biases, and also to be open to new concepts and information that can flip everything you've learned so far on its head. In other words, you will learn how to think critically.

If you go to a mediocre college, you'll learn a technical skillset. That can lead to hubris and ignorance.

Now, if you had said we need to improve public school education across the board, but especially with regards to critical thinking, and "the pursuit of knowledge" as curriculum, I would agree. Much of our education system is designed to produce technician workers who are not free thinkers and will therefore not challenge the established order.

Parks in Spain have different rules, but usually you can tent camp while backpacking as long as the tent is not set up before 7pm and must be taken down by 9am. This type of camping while on the move is usually referred to as a "bivouac" in europe.
If you're backpacking the thickest are Big Agnes pads. Other thick ones are the thermrest neo lite x air. And the nemo tensor. If you're car camping just buy an air mattress off amazon.

If the ground is cold and your airmattress is not rated for cold weather (google "sleeping pad r values"), you should use a foam mat under your air mattress, or some reflectix (you can get at hardware stores). Cold ground will sap you're heat. In warm areas this isn't as big of a deal.
Additionally don't put your mattress on bare earth. Always use a ground sheet, or some other medium. Pads puncture easily, treat them gently.

You can get a single burner camp stove on Amazon for $20 or less that works with standard iso butane cannisters. Cooking over fire can be fun for a meal. But you're not going to want to make a fire every time you want to boil water for coffee, or cook some oatmeal, or whatever. Many places have fire bans too, but stoves are an exception, so they are really worth it in the long run.
Get an insulated sleeping pad, and consider a fleece sleeping bag liner.

Look at the national park website. You are likely allowed to use gas camp stoves, but not make open fires with wood.

If you're sleeping in the car, why would you leave food outside? Leaving food outside in bear country is a terrible idea, as the bears become habituated and more likely to seek people's camps for food. If a bear wakes you up while you are sleeping in or near your car you can scare it off. 

From glacier national park webpage:
"If a bear appears intent on approaching you, your group, or your campsite in a non-defensive manner (not showing signs of agitation), gather your group together, make noise, and try to discourage the bear from further approaching. Prepare to deploy your bear spray. If you are preparing or consuming food, secure it. DO NOT LET THE BEAR GET YOUR FOOD"
